name: Stroke Warning Signs
source_guidance: Adapted from the NHS FAST stroke campaign (Face, Arms, Speech, Time) and WHO guidance on stroke recognition.

questions.text: Has the person collapsed, or are they unresponsive or having a fit?
Face: has one side of the face suddenly dropped, or can they not smile evenly?
Arms: is there sudden weakness or numbness in one arm or leg, or can they not lift both arms and keep them up?
Speech: is their speech suddenly slurred or muddled, or can they not understand what is said?
Is there sudden loss of vision, sudden severe dizziness or loss of balance, or a sudden very severe headache?
Did any of these signs start in the last 24 hours, even if they have now gone?
Did signs like these happen in the past week but have now fully gone?
Has numbness or tingling come on slowly over weeks, with no sudden change?

emergency: Call 112 now, or get to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Note the time the symptoms started, or when the person was last seen well. Tell the hospital this time.
Do not give food, drink, or medicine by mouth in case swallowing is affected.
Do not wait to see if the symptoms go away. Do not take the person to a traditional healer or place of worship first.
Lay the person on their side if they are drowsy or vomiting.
urgent: Go to a hospital today to be checked for a mini-stroke (TIA), even though the signs have gone.
Take a list of current medicines, including any for blood pressure or diabetes.
If any stroke sign comes back, call 112 immediately.
routine: Book a clinic appointment within the next few days.
Ask for a blood pressure and blood sugar check.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
self_care: No stroke warning signs were found.
Learn the FAST signs: Face dropping, Arm weakness, Speech problems, Time to call 112.
Keep blood pressure checks and medicines up to date.
Call 112 at once if any sudden weakness, face drooping, or speech problem appears.
